preamble: Assibilation of /d/ before a high front vowel or /j/ to the voiced alveolo-palatal affricate /dʑ/. Japanese /di/ became [dʑi] in the Late Middle Japanese period, and the result later merged with /zi/ (the yotsugana merger). In Slavic, Proto-Balto-Slavic *dj gave Serbo-Croatian đ /dʑ/, and in Polish palatalized (soft) *d became dź /dʑ/ around the 12th century.

examples.note: In Late Middle Japanese (12th–16th centuries) /t, d/ affricated before /i, u/: /ti, di/ became [tɕi, dʑi] and /tu, du/ became [tsu, dzu]. In Standard Japanese ぢ is now pronounced like じ.
The *dj cluster coalesced into /dʑ/ (spelled đ, Cyrillic ђ). Compare Polish miedza from the same source.
Soft *t and *d became the alveolo-palatal affricates ć and dź in Polish in the 12th century.

sources: Wikipedia (2026). History of Polish: soft *t, *d > ć, dź (after Klemensiewicz, Lehr-Spławiński & Urbańczyk 1965). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Polish
